description: How identities are shaped, the diverse make-up of the UK and the value of mutual respect.
content_html:
What Is the United Kingdom?

The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland is made up of four nations: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Each nation has its own distinct culture, language traditions, history and, in some cases, its own devolved government. Scotland has the Scottish Parliament, Wales has the Senedd (the Welsh Parliament) and Northern Ireland has the Northern Ireland Assembly. England does not have its own separate parliament; matters affecting only England are generally decided by the UK Parliament at Westminster. This four-nation structure means that questions of national identity are especially complex in the UK: someone may identify simultaneously as Welsh, British and European — a phenomenon known as multiple identities.

Key Fact

The UK consists of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland each have their own devolved legislature (Scottish Parliament, Senedd and Northern Ireland Assembly). England does not have a separate parliament.

What Shapes Our Identities?

Identity is shaped by a wide range of factors operating at different levels. At the individual level, a person’s sense of self is influenced by family background, religion, language, ethnicity, gender, class and personal experience. At the group level, people form shared identities through membership of communities — a faith community, a sports club, a neighbourhood, a professional group. At the national level, institutions such as Parliament, the NHS and the legal system, as well as shared historical events and cultural traditions, contribute to a sense of belonging to the UK. At the global level, shared religion, language communities (such as the Commonwealth) and shared global causes also form part of many people’s identity.

Importantly, identity is not fixed. It shifts over time as people’s circumstances, relationships and experiences change. A teenager living in Cardiff might feel strongly Welsh, British and European all at once; the same person at a different stage of life might place different emphasis on different aspects of their identity. Citizenship studies recognise that this fluidity is normal and that having multiple identities does not mean there is any conflict between them.

The Diverse Nature of the UK Population

The UK has a long history of diversity. Over centuries, waves of migration have brought people from across Europe, Asia, Africa, the Caribbean and beyond, each contributing to the cultural, economic and social fabric of the country. According to the 2021 Census for England and Wales, around 18% of the population described themselves as belonging to an ethnic group other than White British. The UK is also religiously diverse: Christianity remains the most commonly stated religion, but significant communities practise Islam, Hinduism, Sikhism, Judaism and Buddhism, alongside a growing proportion of people who identify as having no religion.

Diversity in the UK encompasses not only ethnicity and religion but also language (over 300 languages are spoken in London alone), age, disability, sexual orientation and gender identity. The Equality Act 2010 protects nine “protected characteristics” in law: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation.

Key Fact

The Equality Act 2010 lists nine protected characteristics: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation. Discrimination on any of these grounds is unlawful.

Mutual Respect and Understanding

Mutual respect is one of the core values of British civic life. It means recognising that other people have the right to hold different beliefs, follow different cultural practices and live differently, as long as they do not harm others or breach the law. In practice, mutual respect is embedded in laws against hate crime, in equality legislation and in public sector duties to promote equality of opportunity.

The democratic values that underpin British society — the rule of law, individual liberty and democratic participation — depend on mutual respect to function. If citizens refuse to accept the legitimacy of others’ participation in public life, democratic institutions are weakened. Schools, courts, local councils and community organisations all play a role in promoting understanding and building social cohesion.

Supporters of multiculturalism argue that diversity strengthens society: different cultural perspectives foster creativity, economic dynamism and cultural exchange. They point to examples of communities that have enriched British life — in art, food, sport, science and public service — and argue that celebrating cultural difference is more honest and inclusive than expecting all citizens to adopt a single dominant cultural identity. They argue that the Equality Act 2010 and the Human Rights Act 1998 provide the legal framework needed to protect individuals while sustaining diversity.

Critics of multiculturalism argue that if too much emphasis is placed on group identities and cultural differences, it can make it harder to build the shared civic values needed for a cohesive society. Some argue that a stronger emphasis on a single, shared national identity would reduce social fragmentation and help everyone feel they belong. Others point to specific policy debates — for example, around language education for new arrivals, or the teaching of shared history in schools — as areas where a lack of common ground can create tension. Examiners expect students to present both viewpoints without endorsing either as the correct answer.

Some students assume that a person who identifies strongly with their ethnic heritage, religion or regional background is somehow less committed to being British. Citizenship studies reject this assumption. Multiple identities are the norm for most people: a person can feel deeply proud of their Scottish heritage, their Muslim faith and their British citizenship all at once. These identities reinforce rather than compete with one another in most people’s experience. The concept of multiple identities is explicitly taught in the specification precisely because it reflects the reality of life in the contemporary UK.

Why Diversity Matters for Democracy

A diverse society is not without challenges. Discrimination, prejudice and hate crime remain real problems that the law seeks to address. At the same time, diversity is also a strength: exposure to different perspectives can improve decision-making, challenge assumptions and produce more creative solutions to shared problems. A democracy that genuinely represents all its citizens — including those from minority ethnic backgrounds, different faiths, and all regions of the UK — is more likely to make decisions that are fair and sustainable in the long run.
exam_tip_html: On a 12-mark “Evaluate” question about diversity or identity, students often produce a one-sided answer that either celebrates diversity uncritically or focuses only on its challenges. To reach the Mastering band, you must present both perspectives with roughly equal weight, naming specific legislation (for example the Equality Act 2010) or a real demographic fact (such as the 2021 Census data on ethnicity) on each side. Your conclusion must be substantiated: state which argument you find more convincing and explain precisely why, using the evidence you have presented. For an 8-mark “Discuss” question, use connectives (“however,” “on the other hand”) to show that you are genuinely engaging with both views rather than simply listing points.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The UK is made up of four nations, each with distinct identities; Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland each have devolved legislatures, while England does not have its own parliament.
  • Identity is formed at individual, group, national and global levels and most people hold multiple identities simultaneously — this is normal and does not imply disloyalty.
  • Diversity in the UK is protected by the Equality Act 2010, and mutual respect is a civic value underpinning democracy; the debate between multiculturalism and a shared national identity is a contested political question that must be presented with balanced viewpoints.

practice_questions.text:
Which devolved body is responsible for making laws in Wales?
A) The Northern Ireland Assembly
B) The Scottish Parliament
C) The Senedd
D) The House of Lords
State what is meant by the term 'multiple identities'.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks. 1 mark for a basic statement that individuals can hold more than one identity at the same time (e.g. 'a person can be both Welsh and British'). 2 marks for a developed statement that explains the concept more fully (e.g. 'the idea that individuals can belong simultaneously to more than one cultural, national, ethnic or social group, so that a person might identify as British, Muslim and a Londoner all at once').

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which the UK population is diverse.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per way (1 for a basic point, 2 for a developed point with additional detail).

Acceptable points include:
- Ethnic diversity: the 2021 Census for England and Wales found around 18% of the population described themselves as belonging to an ethnic group other than White British; communities with heritage from South Asia, the Caribbean, Africa, East Asia and Eastern Europe all contribute to UK life.
- Religious diversity: while Christianity is the most stated religion, significant communities practise Islam, Hinduism, Sikhism, Judaism and Buddhism; the proportion identifying as having no religion has grown substantially.
- Linguistic diversity: over 300 languages are spoken in London alone, reflecting the range of migration patterns.
- Diversity in age, disability, sexual orientation and gender identity, all protected under the Equality Act 2010.

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below and answer the question that follows.

A fictional civic research organisation published the following in a 2023 report: "A survey of 2,000 young people aged 15-24 across the UK found that 63% said they felt proud of at least two different aspects of their identity (e.g. their nationality and their cultural heritage). Only 14% said they felt their different identities ever conflicted with one another."

What does the extract suggest about how young people in the UK experience multiple identities? Use the extract and your own knowledge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for accurately identifying what the source shows (most young people feel proud of multiple identities; very few experience conflict between them); 1 mark for interpreting the significance of this (the data challenges the assumption that having more than one identity leads to tension or disloyalty); 1 mark for using own knowledge to develop the point (e.g. the concept of multiple identities from the citizenship specification; the four-nation structure of the UK; or the Equality Act 2010 protecting multiple characteristics); 1 mark for a substantiated judgement (e.g. the source suggests that multiple identities are a normal feature of contemporary British life, though the sample is limited to young people and may not represent all age groups).

practice_questions.text:
A local council is planning a community event to celebrate the diversity of its population. A group of residents argues that celebrating different cultural identities risks creating division rather than unity.

Discuss whether celebrating diversity in a community strengthens or weakens social cohesion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced two-sided discussion using connectives to weigh contrasting perspectives. Names at least one specific piece of legislation (Equality Act 2010) or a real-world example. Considers the case that celebrating diversity strengthens cohesion (building trust between communities, reflecting the genuine make-up of society, promoting mutual respect) alongside the argument that it might risk emphasising differences over shared values. Reaches a substantiated position that weighs the arguments.

Secure (5-6 marks): Both perspectives present and broadly accurate, with at least one named reference. Generally balanced. Connectives used.

Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points on at least one side; limited development; little or no named example.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic statements about diversity or community; largely descriptive; no real-world example.

practice_questions.text:
A national newspaper editorial argues: 'A shared national identity is more important than celebrating cultural differences when it comes to building a united UK.'

Evaluate whether promoting a shared national identity is the most effective way to build social cohesion in the UK.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): Full two-sided argument. Arguments for a shared national identity might include: shared civic values (democracy, rule of law) give all citizens a common framework regardless of background; a stronger emphasis on shared history and institutions can reduce fragmentation; some commentators argue that multiculturalism has in some places weakened common civic ties. Arguments against might include: the UK has always been a multi-nation state with distinct Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish identities; the Equality Act 2010 and Human Rights Act 1998 reflect a commitment to protecting difference rather than erasing it; diversity in itself strengthens democratic decision-making and economic creativity; 2021 Census data shows the UK population is more diverse than ever, meaning a single-identity approach may exclude significant communities. Substantiated conclusion weighs which approach better promotes genuine social cohesion and explains why, with reference to named examples.

Secure (7-9 marks): Both sides present and mostly accurate. At least one named legislation or institution per side. Conclusion present.

Developing (4-6 marks): Relevant points but one-sided or under-developed. Some real-world reference. Conclusion thin or absent.

Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic statements. Largely descriptive. No substantiated judgement.

glossary_terms.definition: The idea that individuals can belong to more than one cultural, national, ethnic or social group at the same time.
A person's sense of who they are, formed by a combination of personal, social, cultural and national factors.
The existence within a society of a wide variety of cultural, ethnic, religious, linguistic and social groups.
A commitment to acknowledging and valuing the rights and dignity of others, even where views and backgrounds differ.
The degree to which different groups in a society live alongside one another in a spirit of respect and shared civic belonging.
A social model in which different cultural, ethnic and religious groups coexist and are encouraged to maintain their distinct identities within a shared civic framework.

items.description: An engaging look at how national identity and borders are constructed — useful context for understanding why identity in the UK (with four nations) is so complex.

items.description: Explores how diverse societies represent all their citizens through democratic systems — links to the lesson's theme of diversity strengthening democracy.

items.title: Bend It Like Beckham (2002)
items.description: A British-Asian teenager navigates cultural identity, family expectations and her own ambitions — a warm, funny exploration of what it means to hold multiple identities at once.

items.title: Hidden Figures (2016)
items.description: The true story of Black women mathematicians who worked at NASA in the 1960s — shows how diversity of background and experience drove breakthroughs in a homogeneous institution.
